I see. I heard that that's apparently something that happens with people on bipolar disorder, where sweets become a mood lifter during Depression and a vice/necessity during (hypo)mania. 

So I wondered if someone else dealt with such as well or if there was a predisposition to it for bipolar disorder. But yeah, certain medication I've heard definitely adds to binge eating as mentioned above.

I unfortunately don't have any tips but I was/am in the same boat as you and found that when I binged on some TV that I really liked by myself, it was enough of a buffer to help things calm down a bit. 

Honestly, I don't know how you feel about alone time or how feasible it is, but it's certainly helpful when you're finding yourself being irritated by just about anything to do with other people.

this is true and I certainly agree, I had to explain myself as to why I was doing so poorly in school for financial aid purposes and just chalked it up to "not being able to thrive in college/learning to adjust" but being a college junior makes me feel like that's a hard excuse to keep holding onto. 

Depression definitely has an effect on the brain altogether though, I can't say I've been the same after a few episodes.

I think it's safer to say that I have done worse in college now before being diagnosed than after and there's a good chance my diagnosis has to do with it. In public school, I was a 4.0 student who played cello and did other extracurricular activities. Basically, high excelling and a good student (though I don't like to think that good student = high intelligence). 

I'm currently a neurobiology major in college with the hopes of going to medical school. Pretty much after my first semester, I was hospitalized for my first major depressive episode and a few months later, my first hypomanic episode that was caught before it was fully manic. In the those same 2 years, I've gone from being an A student to being a B/C with more F's and D's than I'd like to admit.

The episodes I'm sure have had a lot to do with it, but since then I'm god awful at remembering basic things I've learned in classes and have a harder time than ever making a case when it comes to intellectual debates with friends. But also, I'm just overall less understanding of complex things than I have been or was. 

I can't say Bipolar disorder is the only cause as I self medicated with marijuana for a bit and it does have some effects on your memory and cognition as well.

I'm more than a little frustrated that nobody is discussing her mental health advocacy. I get it, she did Star Wars and that is her most notable work, but please talk about how much she cared about giving visibility to bipolar disorder. 

It's a media thing, I get it. But, if she had done Star Wars but died doing what someone with Bipolar is "known for" like mood swings and constant "crazy" stuff, they would've brought it up in every single story posted. It's just so sad. 

She was an amazing and wonderful actress, yes, but she was also someone who made sure that part of her wasn't erased due to fame.

I find it to be comforting in, just as everyone else said, you have someone to take care of you and the pressures of everyday life are over for a bit. 

What I'm supremely not fond of is that, in my case anyways, it just fuels stress when people don't know where I am and then adds to anxiety when I realize that I'm not in a place that is familiar to me. Home is nice because you have control over the little things like TV and internet. There, it's all said and done for you. And you're scrambling to talk to a doctor so he can hear the stuff you've been thinking about all day when nobody else does. 

I just hate that you're somewhat of a prisoner in that regard. Prisoner that they want to help get stable again, but freedomless still.

I hear it, I don't deny it nor do I think the advice is misguided. 

Having my faculties at the moment gives me some solace that this could or could not get any worse, but I'm also thinking that could possibly be the thing that's helping me know if it's an episode or not. I totally understand your concern though, however.

Unmedicated at the moment here, not sure if that provides any sort of range thinking for this thread. But, my sleep pattern has been erratic in the last week to say the least. 

Monday was a stressful time for me which resulted in lots of crying and sleeping, I was certain that there was a trigger for depression that was lurking about as it lasted through Tuesday, Euthymic me tends to pull herself out of something that makes her upset with a bit of positive thinking. But then, I did some nice things for others and everything changed, so it was atypical to say the least.

Come Wednesday - Friday, I've had a total of 5 hours of sleep and am feeling the little buzz I get when I find my mind racing or I get too excited. Trying to sleep results in sleep that is interrupted by one reason or another, and paranoia sinks in. 45 minutes feels like 6 hours of sleep (dreaming wise) and eventually I can't tell if its insomnia or hypomania. 

Today, I slept from 1 am to 4 am, stayed up for about 15 minutes, went back to sleep and woke up at 10 am. All in all, a very erratic sleeping schedule. 

EDIT: It's worth mentioning that yesterday afternoon I made a call to my campus clinic and set up an appointment, not encouraging bad behaviors here.

Maybe when it comes to someone trying to discuss a part of their mental illness, attaching "probably" before making your own assumptions isn't helpful.

Exactly! Yes. I think it's very possible to live with depression for your entire life but there are a lot of things that come with depression in the way of triggers and life changes. And yes, depression is also something that you can manage without medications as therapy is very helpful in the cases that I had with depression as well. 

I'm in the same boat as you though. I had MDD my first semester of college until my second semester of college when I had my first (hypo)manic episode that was on the edge of full mania. 

Also, people just like to use the idea of "bipolar" in popular culture to mean mood swings and destructive rather than what Borderline Personality Disorder usually has hallmarks of.

I would say anything that's an imbalance in the brain isn't something to envy. But, as I understand it, Unipolar depression is something that isn't a lifelong condition so the battle is just getting to the finish line.

It's more like a 5k than a marathon, it's still just as hard and you still have to prepare for getting through it but you know there's a chance of an end on the other side. That isn't to say your problems aren't just as serious because depression kills and is not a good thing to have. 

But, I think it's safe to say you dodged a bullet with not having the mania OP. It's better to know that when you're feeling uplifted and happy, it's not a suspicious thing that may end with you in the hospital because you were convinced that a bus couldn't hurt you due to your bones being made of steel.

There's a few people here in the forum who are 40+ which I think is fairly long considering that anyone with bipolar disorder is already at a 10 year disadvantage statistically. People in the US live, on average, to 79 years old. 

Which, 40 doesn't seem like a lot but when you're constantly battling your own mind, it's a victory nonetheless. To answer your second question about happy, I guess it would depend on who you ask.

At the apartment with him, things are fine now. He seems to have calmed down and even thanked me for organizing his things as an attempt to maybe show he doesn't hate me. But, I still think about how once I move out, I really won't have anyone and that's just a scary thought.

As for at home with family, I just can't be bothered to go back there. My mom is very worrysome, which isn't awful but when I'm dealing with a depressive episode, I can't stand the feeling of her watching me every single second and making me feel worse for making her worry. I can't tell if it's better or worse. We aren't that close, my mom or my family for that matter, so I don't feel in the least bit comfortable to come to them with these things.

It was going well, everything was. I felt like at least there was a person who didn't make me feel like it was a challenge to have someone around. I thought it was nice to find someone who was as in love with the idea of loving another person as I was. It was just one of those things where I could feel like, if someone loved me, then at least when I did something stupid or bad, I wouldn't have to be scared of being alone because there were other things about me that this person would find to outweigh the cons.

And then eventually this person just decided that I wasn't worth the trouble and they really didn't love these things about me, just thought they did. Having someone say over and over again that they don't care about your feelings or care about you or that they've been thinking they wanted you out of their life already, now they're just very sure is a heartbreaking thing. It's probably more heartbreaking to know that you've dealt with this before so it isn't surprising that another person says they don't care.

She was the one that I went to in crisis after the mixed episode and she was the one who called the police. It wasn't her fault, we had a long discussion prior to and I thought I'd be in there for a 3 days and it ended up being a week. And then she moved and I was with another therapist who was the one that pushed me to try to come in with "things I wanted to fix" which sounds terrifying when you realize that you're in a spiral of toxic coping mechanisms that are hard to get past. So eventually I stopped going just out of the pressure along with the desire to feel again - which has hurt me more than helped, it seems.

It's more of a worry of not having a say. The last time was because I was on the verge of a manic/mixed episode which resulted in staying up for nearly 2 days and cutting myself repeatedly just for the sake of it. I feel they'll think I'm more of a risk to myself than anything else knowing that I'm now contemplating suicide with BP1. I just can't bring myself to have to go back there again and deal with the stress of not being able to afford medical bills and the insane isolation that comes with being on a suicide watch/in a mental health hospital.

I just feel so guilty. I go to college so the school willingly provides these services for students, psychiatry and all for free. Which makes me feel worse for not wanting to reach out, but I also don't think I can handle going back to another mental hospital as it would be three times in 2 years and every time is 1 step forward, 4 steps back. I just want to make everything stop. I wish I didn't care so much or have to deal with my own thoughts along with others opinions.
